Cartography of tea

From Testipedia, the free encyclopedia
This article is about the diagrams. For the drink, see Tea.
Maps drawn of tea-growing regions

Tea cartography is the practice of drawing the terraces, roads and drying sheds of a tea-growing district on a single sheet, so that a buyer can see at a glance where a lot came from.[1] The earliest surviving examples are estate plans, drawn for owners rather than for readers, and they show boundaries far more carefully than they show terrain.

Modern versions borrow from soil science: a contemporary sheet will usually carry an elevation band, a rainfall figure and a harvest window alongside the outline of each plot.[2] Nothing about the convention is standardised, which is part of why two maps of the same valley can disagree so completely about where it ends.

Origins

[edit]

The first estate plans were commissioned as legal documents, and the surveyors who drew them worked from chain measurements rather than from any instrument that could record height. Terraces therefore appear as flat bands.

Estate plans

[edit]

An estate plan names every plot and gives its area, because the area is what the owner was taxed on. Roads are drawn only where a cart could actually pass.

Regional styles

[edit]

Assamese sheets are drawn north-up and lean on river courses; Yunnan sheets are drawn valley-up, with the ridge line at the top of the page, which reads as upside-down to anyone trained on the former.

  • North-up sheets favour rivers as their organising line.
  • Valley-up sheets favour ridges, and put altitude before direction.

Tools

[edit]

Since the 1990s most sheets begin life in a geographic information system, and the hand-drawn ones are redrawn from aerial imagery rather than from a survey done on foot. The convention has outlived the method.
